citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume AC. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then $$\Phi_X(t):=\mathbb E e^{it\cdot X}=\exp(it\cdot m-t^T\Sigma t/2)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R^d).$$ This transform uniquely determines the law, including singular Sigma.

Assume AC. Every second-countable locally compact Hausdorff space is Polish,
hence standard Borel. Consequently, if $G$ is a second-countable locally
compact Hausdorff topological group and $H\le G$ is a closed subgroup, then
the homogeneous space $G/H$ with its quotient topology is Polish and the
quotient Borel structure together with the left action
$G\times G/H\to G/H$ is a standard Borel $G$-space with Borel action.

A topological space $X$ is **second countable** when its topology has a basis $\mathcal B$ that is at most countable ([[def-topology-basis-subbasis]], [[def-countable]]). Thus every open set is a union of members of one at most countable family $\mathcal B$.

A topological space $(X, \mathcal{T})$ ([[def-topological-space]]) is **locally
compact** when

> every point of $X$ has a compact neighbourhood:

that is, for every $x \in X$ there is a neighbourhood $N$ of $x$
([[def-neighbourhood-top]]) that is a compact subset of $X$
([[def-compact-space]], [[def-subspace-topology-top]]).

**A neighbourhood need not be open here**, and that is what makes the condition
the weak one it is meant to be: $N$ is required only to contain some open set
containing $x$. Writing "compact **open** neighbourhood" instead would define a
strictly stronger property, satisfied by no space in which a point has no compact
open neighbourhood, $\mathbb{R}$ among them; and requiring the compact set merely
to *contain* $x$ would define a property so weak that every space with a
singleton has it, singletons being compact.

**Every compact space is locally compact**, since $X$ itself is a neighbourhood
of each of its points and is a compact subset of itself. The converse fails, and
$\mathbb{R}^n$ is the standard witness.

**What the condition says in a metric space.** Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space
carrying its metric topology ([[def-metric-topology]], [[def-metrizable-space]]),
with balls as in [[def-metric-ball]], and let $x \in X$. Then

> $x$ has a compact neighbourhood **if and only if** there are a real $r > 0$ and
> a compact $K \subseteq X$ with $B(x,r) \subseteq K$.

*Both directions are immediate and are discharged here.* If $N$ is a compact
neighbourhood of $x$, fix an open $U$ with $x \in U \subseteq N$; by
[[def-metric-topology]] there is $r > 0$ with $B(x,r) \subseteq U \subseteq N$, so
$K := N$ serves. Conversely, if $B(x,r) \subseteq K$ with $K$ compact, then $K$
contains the open set $B(x,r)$, which contains $x$, so $K$ is a neighbourhood of
$x$ and is compact. Compactness of a subset of $(X,d)$ means the same thing read
metrically and read topologically
([[thm-compactness-agrees-with-metric-compactness]]), so the criterion may be
applied with either development's theorems.

**$\mathbb{R}^n$ is locally compact for every $n \ge 1$.** Give $\mathbb{R}^n$
the product topology, which is the metric topology of the Euclidean metric $d_2$
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[cor-heine-borel-in-the-product-topology]]). For
$p \in \mathbb{R}^n$ the set

$$Q_p \;:=\; \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : d_2(x,p) \le 1 \,\}$$

is closed, being the complement of the union of the open balls $B(y, d_2(y,p) - 1)$
over the points $y$ with $d_2(y,p) > 1$, and it is bounded
([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]), lying inside $B(p, 2)$; so $Q_p$ is compact by
[[cor-heine-borel-in-the-product-topology]]. It contains the open ball $B(p,1)$,
which contains $p$, so it is a compact neighbourhood of $p$. The space
$\mathbb{R}^n$ is not compact, so local compactness is strictly weaker than
compactness.

Define $d_{\mathbb{R}} : \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ by
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) := |x - y|$ ([[def-abs-value]]). Then:

1. $d_{\mathbb{R}}$ is a metric on $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-metric-space]]); it is
   called the **usual metric** of $\mathbb{R}$.
2. For $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and $r > 0$ the open ball is the bounded open interval
   ([[def-interval]], [[def-metric-ball]])
   $$B(x,r) = (x-r,\ x+r),$$
   and the closed ball is $\bar B(x,r) = [x-r,\ x+r]$.
3. Consequently $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is open in the metric topology of
   $d_{\mathbb{R}}$ ([[def-metric-topology]]) exactly when for every $x \in U$
   there is $r > 0$ with $(x-r, x+r) \subseteq U$. This topology is called the
   **usual topology** of $\mathbb{R}$.
4. $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ is not a bounded metric space
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]): no ball contains $\mathbb{R}$, so
   $\operatorname{diam}(\mathbb{R})$ is not defined.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

$\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the rationals are
countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

**No choice principle is used.** The one place where a reader expects a choice,
"pick a representative $a/b$ of each rational", is exactly where
[[lem-rat-positive-denominator]] applies: every rational *has* a representative
with positive denominator, so the map $(a,b) \mapsto [(a,b)]$ defined on
$\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is already **surjective** onto $\mathbb{Q}$,
and countability follows from a surjection without ever selecting a
representative. The same device handles $\mathbb{Z}$, which is a surjective image
of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ by construction ([[def-integers]]).

The map $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[def-real-numbers]]) is an embedding of ordered
fields. Every real is approximated by rationals: for $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and
rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $q \in \mathbb{Q}$ with
$|x - \hat q| < \hat\varepsilon$. Consequently, strictly between any two
reals lies a rational.

If $A$ and $B$ are at most countable ([[def-countable]]) then so is
$A \times B$.

**No choice principle is used**: the two enumerations are given, and the
enumeration of the product is written down from them.

Let $(E_i,\mathcal E_i)_{i\in I}$ be measurable spaces. A family
$(\mu_F)_{F\Subset I}$, indexed by all finite subsets of $I$, is a **consistent family of finite-dimensional
distributions** when each $\mu_F$ is a probability measure on
$\bigotimes_{i\in F}\mathcal E_i$, with the finite unordered product
sigma-algebra of [[def-coordinate-maps-and-cylinder-sigma-algebra]], and for
every pair of finite sets $F\subseteq G\subseteq I$ the pushforward of
$\mu_G$ under the restriction $p_{G,F}(x)=x|_F$ equals $\mu_F$; equivalently,
$\mu_G(p_{G,F}^{-1}(A))=\mu_F(A)$ for every
$A\in\bigotimes_{i\in F}\mathcal E_i$. The restriction is measurable since
inverse images of coordinate generators are coordinate generators. The empty
support carries the unique probability measure on the singleton empty product.

Reordering means choosing a different enumeration of the **same** finite set
$F$. If $e:[n]\to F$ is an enumeration, its displayed ordered law is the
pushforward of $\mu_F$ under $r_e(x)=(x_{e(0)},\ldots,x_{e(n-1)})$.
For another enumeration $e'$, the coordinate permutation $r_{e'}\circ r_e^{-1}$
pushes this ordered law to the one displayed using $e'$. This is automatic
from these definitions and does not require equal laws on different subsets
of $I$, or invariance under permutations of a fixed ordered product.
In particular, consistency is data about
every finite joint law, not merely the one-coordinate marginals.

For measurable spaces $(E_i,\mathcal E_i)_{i\in I}$, put
$E=\prod_{i\in I}E_i$. For finite $F\subseteq I$, let
$\pi_F:E\to\prod_{i\in F}E_i$ be restriction to $F$ (the singleton empty
product when $F=\varnothing$). On $\prod_{i\in F}E_i$, write $q_i$ for the
$i$th coordinate map and define

$$\bigotimes_{i\in F}\mathcal E_i:=\sigma\{q_i^{-1}(A):i\in F,\ A\in\mathcal E_i\}.$$

For $F=\varnothing$ this is the two-set sigma-algebra on the singleton. If
$e:[n]\to F$ is any enumeration, coordinate relabelling identifies this
sigma-algebra with the recursively defined finite product sigma-algebra of
[[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]: both are
generated by the same coordinate inverse images. Thus the notation is
independent of the enumeration.

A **finite-coordinate cylinder** is $\pi_F^{-1}(A)$ for
$A\in\bigotimes_{i\in F}\mathcal E_i$. The **cylinder sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal C_I:=\sigma\{\pi_F^{-1}(A):F\subseteq I\text{ finite},\ A\in\bigotimes_{i\in F}\mathcal E_i\}.$$

This is the product sigma-algebra on the arbitrary product; the empty-support cylinder is either $\varnothing$ or $E$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For any set $I$, standard-Borel coordinate spaces $(E_i,\mathcal E_i)$, and consistent finite-dimensional laws $(\mu_F)_{F\Subset I}$, there is a unique probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathcal C_I$ whose $F$-coordinate marginal is $\mu_F$ for each finite $F$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. A real stochastic process
$X=(X_t)_{t\in I}$ [[def-stochastic-process-and-finite-dimensional-distributions]]
is a **Gaussian process** if, for every integer $n\ge 1$, every time list
$t_1,\ldots,t_n\in I$, and every $a_1,\ldots,a_n\in\mathbb R$, the random
variable
$$
\sum_{j=1}^n a_jX_{t_j}
$$
has a normal law $N(m,\sigma^2)$ for some $m\in\mathbb R$ and
$\sigma\ge0$. Variance zero is allowed, so constant linear combinations are
included.

Equivalently, for every such time list the evaluation vector
$(X_{t_1},\ldots,X_{t_n})$ has a possibly singular multivariate normal law in
the sense of [[def-multivariate-normal-law]]. Indeed, that definition says
exactly that every scalar projection of the vector is normal. This also covers
repeated times, zero coefficients, and singular covariance matrices; no
distinct-time convention is needed for this definition.

Choice is declared because the library's scalar and multivariate normal-law
interfaces construct their probability laws and independent standard-normal
realizations under AC. The equivalence itself is only an unpacking of the
finite-dimensional projection definition and makes no further selection.

Let $T\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, $d\ge1$, have its relative Borel sigma-algebra, and
let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be one probability space. A **real random
field** indexed by $T$ is a family $X=(X(s))_{s\in T}$ of real random variables
$X(s):\Omega\to\mathbb R$ on that space. This is coordinate measurability:
each map $(s,\omega)\mapsto X(s,\omega)$ with $s$ fixed is measurable in
$\omega$. The field is **jointly measurable** when the map
$(s,\omega)\mapsto X(s,\omega)$ from
$(T\times\Omega,\mathcal B(T)\otimes\mathcal F)$ to
$(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$ is measurable. Joint measurability is an
additional hypothesis when a spatial Lebesgue integral is used; it is not part
of coordinate measurability.

Write $\mathcal L(X(s_1),\ldots,X(s_n))$ for the pushforward law of a finite
coordinate tuple ([[def-stochastic-process-and-finite-dimensional-distributions]],
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]). The field is **strictly stationary** on $T$ when, for every
finite tuple $s_1,\ldots,s_n\in T$ and every $u\in\mathbb R^d$ for which
$s_i+u\in T$ for all $i$, these joint laws are invariant under the common
translation $s_i\mapsto s_i+u$. This extends the integer-shift convention for
time series in [[def-strict-and-weak-stationarity-for-time-series]] to spatial
indices.

Write $T-T:=\{t-s:s,t\in T\}$ for the set of displacements realized by pairs
of sites.

The field is **wide stationary** when every $X(s)$ is square-integrable, its
mean is one constant $m$, and there is a function $C:T-T\to\mathbb R$ such
that
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X(s),X(t))=C(t-s)\qquad(s,t\in T).$$
For a wide-stationary field on all of $\mathbb R^d$, it is **wide isotropic**
when $C(h)$ depends only on the Euclidean norm $\|h\|$.

For $h\in T-T$ and any $s$ with $s,s+h\in T$, put
$\Delta_hX(s):=X(s+h)-X(s)$. The field is **intrinsically stationary of order
two** when for each $h\in T-T$ the first and second raw moments of
$\Delta_hX(s)$ are finite and independent of the admissible starting site
$s$. Here these moments are $\mathbb E[\Delta_hX(s)]$ and
$\mathbb E[(\Delta_hX(s))^2]$. The common second moment defines the
**variogram**
$$\gamma(h):=\frac12\mathbb E[(\Delta_hX(s))^2].$$
The mean increment may depend on $h$ and need not be zero; no finite second
moment of the field levels themselves is required by this definition.

derivations.claim: For each nonempty finite $F\subseteq T$, use AC to choose an enumeration $e_F:\{1,\ldots,n_F\}\to F$. Put $t_i=e_F(i)$, $m_F=(m(t_i))_{i=1}^{n_F}$, and $K_F=[K(t_i,t_j)]_{i,j=1}^{n_F}$. Let $r_F:\mathbb R^{n_F}\to\mathbb R^F$ relabel coordinates by $r_F(x)(e_F(i))=x_i$. The matrix $K_F$ is symmetric positive semidefinite by the hypothesis on $K$, so [F1] supplies $N_{n_F}(m_F,K_F)$; define the probability measure on the actual coordinate space by $\mu_F:=(r_F)_\#N_{n_F}(m_F,K_F)$. If $F=\varnothing$, use the unique probability law on the singleton empty product. Changing the enumeration permutes $m_F$ and both indices of $K_F$ by the same permutation. The characteristic-function formula in [F2] shows that the corresponding permutation of $\mathbb R^{n_F}$ carries one Gaussian law to the other; after relabelling, the resulting measure on $\mathbb R^F$ is unchanged. Thus $\mu_F$ is independent of the chosen enumeration.

The intervals $(p,q)$ with rational endpoints form a countable family by the countability of $\mathbb Q$ and [F4]. They form a base: if $U$ is open and $x\in U$, choose $r>0$ with $(x-r,x+r)\subseteq U$; rational density supplies $p,q\in\mathbb Q$ with $x-r<p<x<q<x+r$, so $x\in(p,q)\subseteq U$. Thus $\mathbb R$ is second-countable by [F4]. If $x\ne y$, the open balls about $x$ and $y$ of radius $|x-y|/3$ are disjoint: a point in both would give $|x-y|<2|x-y|/3$ by the triangle inequality. Hence the metric topology is Hausdorff. It is locally compact since each $x$ has the compact interval $[x-1,x+1]$ as a neighborhood by [F4]. Therefore [F3] makes $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$ standard Borel.

Let $F\subseteq H$ be finite and nonempty, and use the enumerations fixed in step 1.1. Write $\pi_{H,F}:\mathbb R^H\to\mathbb R^F$ for restriction. For $u\in\mathbb R^F$, define $\widetilde u\in\mathbb R^{n_H}$ by $\widetilde u_j=u(e_H(j))$ when $e_H(j)\in F$, and $\widetilde u_j=0$ otherwise. Under the coordinate relabelling $r_H$, the characteristic function of $(\pi_{H,F})_\#\mu_H$ at $u$ is the characteristic function of $N_{n_H}(m_H,K_H)$ at $\widetilde u$. By [F2] this is $$\exp\!\left(i\sum_{t\in F}u(t)m(t)-\frac12\sum_{s,t\in F}u(s)u(t)K(s,t)\right).$$ This is also the characteristic function of $\mu_F=(r_F)_\#N_{n_F}(m_F,K_F)$ at $u$, by [F2]. Identifying $\mathbb R^F$ with $\mathbb R^{n_F}$ through $r_F$, uniqueness of characteristic functions in [F2] gives $(\pi_{H,F})_\#\mu_H=\mu_F$. Empty sets give the unique singleton marginal. Hence the family is consistent in the sense of [F5].

The consistent family from step 2.1 now satisfies the standard-Borel hypotheses of [F7]. Kolmogorov extension gives a unique probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathcal C_T$ with the specified finite-coordinate marginals.

On $(\mathbb R^T,\mathcal C_T,\mu)$ define $X(t)(\omega):=\omega(t)$. Each coordinate is measurable by [F6], and for every finite set $F$ its joint law is $\mu_F$ by [F7]. The means and covariances are therefore $m(t)$ and $K(s,t)$ by [F1]. For any finite list $t_1,\ldots,t_n$, possibly with repeated sites, and coefficients $a_1,\ldots,a_n$, collect the distinct sites in $F=\{t_1,\ldots,t_n\}$ and put $b_t:=\sum_{j:t_j=t}a_j$. Then $\sum_j a_jX(t_j)=\sum_{t\in F}b_tX(t)$ is a linear projection of the $F$-coordinate Gaussian vector, so it has a normal law by [F1]. This is the Gaussian-process condition [F8], and the coordinates form a real field by [F9]. The extension supplies only the cylinder sigma-algebra; no continuity or joint-measurability conclusion was used.

boundaries.reason: The empty support carries its unique singleton probability law and creates no coordinate condition.

boundaries.evidence: Statement: If K is the zero kernel, all finite Gaussian marginals are point masses at the specified means; no invertibility is needed.
Statement: For a one-point index set the construction is the ordinary scalar normal law, including zero variance.
Statement: Singular finite covariance matrices are included in the multivariate-normal definition and characteristic-function consistency proof.

Write $T-T:=\{t-s:s,t\in T\}$ for the set of displacements realized by pairs

The field is **wide stationary** when every $X(s)$ is square-integrable, its

that
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X(s),X(t))=C(t-s)\qquad(s,t\in T).$$

when $C(h)$ depends only on the Euclidean norm $\|h\|$.

For $h\in T-T$ and any $s$ with $s,s+h\in T$, put

two** when for each $h\in T-T$ the first and second raw moments of

The mean increment may depend on $h$ and need not be zero; no finite second
moment of the field levels themselves is required by this definition.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Let $X,Y$ be square-integrable real random variables on one probability space.
Then
$$\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathbb E[X^2]-\mathbb E[X]^2,$$
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\mathbb E[XY]-\mathbb E[X]\mathbb E[Y].$$
Moreover, covariance is symmetric and bilinear on finite linear combinations.
On finite full-power-set probability spaces these formulas reduce to the

derivations.claim: Suppose first that $X$ is wide stationary. For every $s,h$, its increments have mean zero because the field mean is constant. Wide stationarity gives $C(h)=\operatorname{Cov}(X(s),X(s+h))$ and $C(-h)=\operatorname{Cov}(X(s+h),X(s))$; covariance symmetry [F3] therefore gives $C(-h)=C(h)$. Both level variances equal $C(0)$, and the cross-covariance in the increment variance is $C(-h)=C(h)$. Thus $$\mathbb E[(X(s+h)-X(s))^2]=\operatorname{Var}(X(s+h)-X(s))=2C(0)-2C(h).$$ Dividing by two gives $\gamma(h)=C(0)-C(h)$.

For arbitrary sites $s_1,\ldots,s_n$, set $Y_i:=X(s_i)-X(0)$. Each $Y_i$ is square-integrable by order-two intrinsic stationarity, since it is an increment from $0$ to $s_i$. Moreover, $Y_i-Y_j=X(s_i)-X(s_j)$, so [F1] gives $$2\gamma(s_i-s_j)=\mathbb E[(Y_i-Y_j)^2].$$ All cross products are integrable because $2|Y_iY_j|\le Y_i^2+Y_j^2$.

Expanding the finite sum from step 1.2 and using $\sum_i a_i=0$ yields $$ \begin{aligned} \sum_{i,j}a_i a_j\gamma(s_i-s_j) &=\frac12\sum_{i,j}a_i a_j\mathbb E[Y_i^2+Y_j^2-2Y_iY_j]\\ &=-\mathbb E\!\left[\left(\sum_i a_iY_i\right)^2\right]\le0. \end{aligned} $$ The two sums containing $Y_i^2$ or $Y_j^2$ vanish because each contains the factor $\sum_i a_i$; the remaining term is the negative expectation of a square. No choice principle is used.

citations.quote:
Let $T\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, $d\ge1$, have its relative Borel sigma-algebra, and
let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be one probability space. A **real random
field** indexed by $T$ is a family $X=(X(s))_{s\in T}$ of real random variables
$X(s):\Omega\to\mathbb R$ on that space. This is coordinate measurability:
each map $(s,\omega)\mapsto X(s,\omega)$ with $s$ fixed is measurable in
$\omega$. The field is **jointly measurable** when the map
$(s,\omega)\mapsto X(s,\omega)$ from
$(T\times\Omega,\mathcal B(T)\otimes\mathcal F)$ to
$(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$ is measurable. Joint measurability is an
additional hypothesis when a spatial Lebesgue integral is used; it is not part
of coordinate measurability.

Write $\mathcal L(X(s_1),\ldots,X(s_n))$ for the pushforward law of a finite
coordinate tuple ([[def-stochastic-process-and-finite-dimensional-distributions]],
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]). The field is **strictly stationary** on $T$ when, for every
finite tuple $s_1,\ldots,s_n\in T$ and every $u\in\mathbb R^d$ for which
$s_i+u\in T$ for all $i$, these joint laws are invariant under the common
translation $s_i\mapsto s_i+u$. This extends the integer-shift convention for
time series in [[def-strict-and-weak-stationarity-for-time-series]] to spatial
indices.

Write $T-T:=\{t-s:s,t\in T\}$ for the set of displacements realized by pairs
of sites.

The field is **wide stationary** when every $X(s)$ is square-integrable, its
mean is one constant $m$, and there is a function $C:T-T\to\mathbb R$ such
that
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X(s),X(t))=C(t-s)\qquad(s,t\in T).$$
For a wide-stationary field on all of $\mathbb R^d$, it is **wide isotropic**
when $C(h)$ depends only on the Euclidean norm $\|h\|$.

For $h\in T-T$ and any $s$ with $s,s+h\in T$, put
$\Delta_hX(s):=X(s+h)-X(s)$. The field is **intrinsically stationary of order
two** when for each $h\in T-T$ the first and second raw moments of
$\Delta_hX(s)$ are finite and independent of the admissible starting site
$s$. Here these moments are $\mathbb E[\Delta_hX(s)]$ and
$\mathbb E[(\Delta_hX(s))^2]$. The common second moment defines the
**variogram**
$$\gamma(h):=\frac12\mathbb E[(\Delta_hX(s))^2].$$
The mean increment may depend on $h$ and need not be zero; no finite second
moment of the field levels themselves is required by this definition.

Let $X=(X(s))_{s\in T}$ be a real random field on one probability space, with
$X(s)\in L^2$ for every $s\in T$, and put
$K(s,t):=\operatorname{Cov}(X(s),X(t))$. Then $K$ is symmetric and positive
semidefinite: for every $n\ge1$, sites $s_1,\ldots,s_n\in T$, and real
$a_1,\ldots,a_n$,
$$\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n a_i a_j K(s_i,s_j)\ge0.$$

Let $X=(X(t))_{t\in\mathbb R^d}$ be order-two intrinsically stationary in the
sense of [[def-random-field-stationarity-covariance-and-variogram]], with
variogram $\gamma(h)=\tfrac12\mathbb E[(X(t+h)-X(t))^2]$. Then for every
$n\ge1$, sites $s_1,\ldots,s_n\in\mathbb R^d$, and real coefficients
$a_1,\ldots,a_n$ with $\sum_i a_i=0$,
$$\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n a_i a_j\gamma(s_i-s_j)\le0.$$
This is conditional negative definiteness over real coefficients. If $X$ is
also wide stationary with covariance function $C$, then
$$\gamma(h)=C(0)-C(h)\qquad(h\in\mathbb R^d).$$
The proof is choice-free.

A **finite probability space** is a pair $(\Omega,w)$ consisting of a finite set $\Omega$ and a function $w:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ such that $w(\omega)\ge0$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$ and
$$\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)=1.$$
The elements of $\Omega$ are **outcomes**. Every subset $A\subseteq\Omega$ is an **event**, and its probability is
$$\mathbb P(A):=\sum_{\omega\in A}w(\omega).$$

An outcome of weight zero remains an outcome. Thus an event can be nonempty and still have probability zero.

A **real random variable** on a finite probability space $(\Omega,w)$ is a function $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$. Its range $X(\Omega)$ is finite. The **distribution** or **law** of $X$ is the finite probability space on $X(\Omega)$ with
$$\mathbb P_X(x):=\mathbb P(\{\omega\in\Omega:X(\omega)=x\}).$$
The weights $\mathbb P_X(x)$ are nonnegative and sum to $1$ because the fibres of $X$ form a finite partition of $\Omega$ ([[thm-finite-additivity-of-probability]]).

The **expectation** of a real random variable $X$ on a finite probability space $(\Omega,w)$ is
$$\mathbb E[X]:=\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}X(\omega)w(\omega).$$
For a real constant $c$, the notation $c$ also denotes the constant random variable $\omega\mapsto c$.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

derivations.claim: If $C$ were a stationary covariance, its matrix at the two sites $0$ and $1$ would be $$M=\begin{pmatrix}C(0)&C(-1)\\C(1)&C(0)\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&1\end{pmatrix}.$$ The covariance-kernel lemma [F2] would make this matrix positive semidefinite, but for $v=(1,-1)^T$, $v^TMv=-2<0$. Hence $C(h)=1+h^2$ is not a stationary covariance.

For any real $a_1,\ldots,a_n$ with $\sum_i a_i=0$ and sites $s_1,\ldots,s_n$, $$\sum_{i,j}a_i a_j(s_i-s_j)^2=-2\left(\sum_i a_i s_i\right)^2\le0.$$ This directly verifies the zero-sum CND inequality for $\gamma(h)=h^2$ and is consistent with [F3].

Define $Z(\omega):=\sqrt2\,\omega$ on $\Omega=\{-1,+1\}$. By the finite space and expectation definitions [F4]–[F6], $$\mathbb E[Z]=\tfrac12\sqrt2-\tfrac12\sqrt2=0,\qquad\mathbb E[Z^2]=\tfrac12(2)+\tfrac12(2)=2.$$

Define $X(t):=tZ$, so every coordinate has finite range and is square-integrable. For any admissible $t,h$, $X(t+h)-X(t)=hZ$, and $$\frac12\mathbb E[(X(t+h)-X(t))^2]=\frac12h^2\mathbb E[Z^2]=h^2,$$ independent of $t$. Its increment mean is also zero, so the stated intrinsic stationarity and variogram claim hold by [F1].
The field mean is zero and $\operatorname{Var}(X(t))=2t^2$ by [F6]–[F7], so its variance is not constant in $t$. Thus this intrinsically stationary field is not wide stationary, as claimed.
